blocks.text: …a question of composure

Conflict situations between the dog and environmental influences have their cause in a lack of experience, in the memory of negative events and in low inherited temperament strength with regard to different stimulus situations. Environmental conflicts have a high potential to trigger panic-like behaviour in the dog and thereby to remove him partially or, in the worst case, completely from our influence.

The basis for everything is basic trust: In unfamiliar situations, our dog must have learned that following us is worthwhile – not because he has to, but because we are reliably the calmest, safest point in every situation.
Gradually introducing the dog to the widest variety of environmental scenarios is the long-term path – accompanied by composure and positive leadership.
What you should know 📋

Environmental conflicts initially occur independently of the behaviour of any people involved. Only as the situation progresses are the dog's reaction patterns very strongly influenced by our behaviour.
Calm walking and our balanced behaviour help our dog find his bearings among environmental influences. We provide safety through composure and remove stress through skilful leadership.

The flight instinct quickly takes over – and the dog becomes impossible to influence. Calling him back before he reaches a safe flight distance is then no longer possible; unpredictable to dangerous situations can result.
Characteristic – Recognising signs of conflict and early stress signals 👁️
Retreating behaviour, panicky pulling on the leash, stiff sitting down or even rearing up on the hind legs are signs that our dog is in conflict with the situation.

Early stress signals – before panic: Slight hesitation in the step, increased body tension, ears laid back, gaze fixed on the source of the stimulus, shallower or faster breathing, mouth closed and pressed shut. These signals show: Our dog is beginning to classify the stimulus as a threat. Now is the best moment to act – not only once he pulls or rears up.
The personal scenario list – building it systematically 📝
We put together a list of all places and scenarios that we could end up in. Categories are: urban scenarios, rural scenarios, open countryside, traffic scenarios and infrastructure scenarios.
Examples: busy roads, stairs, manhole covers, grazing animals, construction machinery, wild animals, bridges and footbridges, public transport, tunnels, busy squares and so on.

For each scenario we keep brief notes: How did our dog react? At what distance was he still relaxed? What helped? These observations make progress visible and help us choose the next training step in a targeted way.
The list is a living document – not a rigid programme. It gives us structure and prevents us from having to rely on chance encounters.
Prioritisation aid – which scenarios should be trained first? 🎯
We prioritise according to two criteria: frequency (how often do we encounter this scenario?) and strength of reaction (how strongly does our dog currently react to it?).
High priority: Scenarios that occur frequently and trigger strong reactions – for example busy roads, bicycles or construction noise. We train these first.
Medium priority: Scenarios that occur occasionally or trigger only moderate reactions – for example manhole covers, bridges or grazing animals.
Low priority: Rare scenarios to which our dog reacts only mildly – or prepared specifically when a particular event (holiday, move) is coming up.
As a general rule: Always begin with the scenario in which our dog already shows first moments of relaxation. Successes at an easy level build the confidence we need for more difficult situations.
Training – basic principles 🦮
We make absolutely sure that all problematic situations are dealt with without time pressure and in absolute calm. The dog is held neither on a short leash nor by the collar.
It is important to notice the first signs of stress and to fluidly meet the dog's need for self-protection – by moving to a sufficient safety distance. At least until our dog signals calming down.

From this observation distance we collect ourselves mentally and let our dog take in the situation. We take time until the dog experiences noticeable calming – simply stand still, or better still: sit down with the dog away from the scene and let him observe and learn.
Anchor commands as calming anchors at a distance ⚓

“Down” and “sit” are more than obedience commands in environmental conflicts – they are calming anchors. A dog that goes into the “down” at a distance involuntarily lowers his body tension. The lying position is physiologically linked with calm.

Prerequisite: Before being used in conflict situations, the command must already be so well established in neutral, low-stimulus environments that the dog carries it out reliably and without hesitation. Only then does it also work as an anchor under stress.
With increasing depth of training, the “down” at a distance can be used earlier and earlier in time – until it finally works as a calming signal at the very first perception of the stimulus.
Toys and treats – redirection before escalation 🎾
In environmental conflicts, toys and treats are active redirection tools. The decisive difference lies in the timing of their use: not after the situation, but already at the first sign of tension.
At the moment we notice early stress signals – before the dog starts to pull or fixate – we calmly and without fuss present the toy or hold out a treat.

This use has a double effect: It directs attention to us instead of the source of the stimulus – and links the beginning of the stress situation with a positive experience: This stimulus = something good is about to happen with my human.

Important: Toys and treats only work as long as the dog is still below his stress threshold. Once panic has broken out, no treat in the world is interesting any more. Therefore: use them early – always use them earlier.
Procedure in detail 🔄
We recognise a situation building up – or our dog suddenly shows stressed, fearful or panicky behaviour because of a stimulus situation in the current environment.
We stay level-headed and leave the situation calmly and fluidly in a free direction – far enough that our dog's behaviour calms down and he comes along with us with little tension.
Having arrived at the safe place, we stand still or sit down. Our dog determines how long we stay – we remain at least until clear relaxation.

In doing so we may speak with our dog, stroke him soothingly and finally confirm with a treat. A closing game or intensive motivation lifts the overall situation into a learning experience that ends positively.
Step by step, we move on to using the toy or the treat earlier and earlier within the situation – in order to redirect the emerging stress state into positive activity sequences as early as possible.

Throughout the entire process, no coercion may be applied to the dog that could be interpreted as acting in the direction of the source of conflict. Every training process absolutely requires a positive, highly motivating conclusion.
We remember 🧠
In training, any coercion in the direction of the source of the problem is to be regarded as reinforcing the problem and must therefore be avoided.
Recognise early stress signals and act immediately – do not wait for pulling or rearing up.
Use anchor commands such as “down” at a safe distance – they lower body tension and give the dog orientation.
Use toys and treats early – as redirection at the first sign of stress, not only as a reward afterwards.
As confidence grows, shorten the distance step by step and use the positive means earlier and earlier in the situation.
Always build up training progress in small steps. Only positive experiences count as training success!
Important notes ⚠️
Avoid any coercion in the direction of the source of the problem – it reinforces fear lastingly.
Avoid speaking loudly, forcing closeness and attempts at persuasion – they lead to even more insecurity.
Avoid keeping the leash short or holding the dog by the collar in stressful situations.
Avoid using treats or toys only after panic has set in – at that point they no longer work.
Avoid steps that come too early – better to stay longer at one distance than to risk a setback.
Avoid negative experiences caused by wanting too much or by wrong reaction patterns.
Avoid ending a training session without positive, motivating confirmation – every session ends with a good experience.
Practical impulse: Use it earlier – always earlier

The aim is not to get your dog through the situation – it is to show him that the stimulus itself is the signal for something good. Start today: Recognise the first glance toward the source of the stimulus and calmly present the treat at exactly that moment. Hitting this moment earlier and earlier is the art – and the most direct path to change.
→ Do I keep a personal scenario list with observations on reaction and progress?
→ Do I train by priority – frequent and highly stressful scenarios first?
→ Do I recognise my dog's early stress signals before he starts to pull or rear up?
→ Do I leave the situation calmly and fluidly – without time pressure, without comment?
→ Do I always keep the leash sufficiently long – no shortening, no holding on?
→ Do I use anchor commands such as “down” at a safe distance as a calming aid?
→ Do I actively use toys and treats as redirection – early enough, before escalation?
→ Do I stay at the safe place at least until my dog is clearly relaxed?
→ Do I build each training step small enough to guarantee exclusively positive conclusions?
→ Every training process ends positively and motivatingly – without exception!
